The recent selloff in technology stocks has raised questions about how much investors are willing to pay for growth, particularly as the cost of expanding AI infrastructure continues to rise. Even established technology companies have not been immune. In late October, Fortinet and ServiceNow suffered steep single-day share-price declines as investors questioned their growth prospects and the potential disruption from artificial intelligence, despite continued demand for enterprise technology. Reuters reported on October 29 that Fortinet lost 26% to a five-month low, marking the top decliner on Wall Street's benchmark index. Large-cap technology stocks occupy an interesting position in this environment. They offer exposure to established businesses outside the largest technology companies, but their market valuations remain sensitive to changes in earnings expectations and spending patterns. For this article, we define large-cap stocks as companies with market capitalizations between $30 billion and $100 billion. Those exceeding $100 billion are classified as mega-cap stocks, which readers can explore separately in our article on the 12 Best Big Tech Stocks to Buy According to Wall Street Analysts.

The pressure has been especially pronounced among companies financing large-scale AI infrastructure projects. CoreWeave's bond-market difficulties and Nebius's efforts to secure additional financing illustrate how the capital requirements of the AI buildout are becoming an important consideration for investors. Nebius, for instance, secured a $3.5 billion financing facility in October to support its data center expansion. The availability and cost of funding are increasingly relevant to assessing the economics of such projects. Established software providers, cybersecurity firms, and semiconductor businesses have different capital requirements, cash-flow profiles, and exposure to AI spending. For investors, this is significant because strong revenue growth alone does not establish whether a company can sustain profitability or justify its valuation.

Why JPMorgan Upgraded Cloudflare Stock

Key Takeaways

Datadog shares sank 13% today as a flat fourth-quarter revenue outlook overshadowed 35% revenue growth and an earnings beat.

Datadog has beaten the top of its revenue guidance four quarters running, so the flat outlook looks like its usual caution.

Rival Dynatrace still guides higher, and Cloudflare reports Thursday.

Datadog's forward P/E was below its five-year average even before the drop.

Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ) beat Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates this morning, and its stock sank 13% anyway.

The problem: a fourth-quarter revenue outlook no higher than the quarter it just reported. If cloud spending is cooling, Dynatrace (DT:NYSE), Datadog's closest listed rival, and Cloudflare (NET:NYSE), which fell alongside Datadog in last week's software selloff, would feel it too.

A big quarter with a flat finish

Datadog's third quarter was strong:

Revenue of $1.20 billion, up 35%, against the $1.14 billion analysts expected

Adjusted EPS of $0.81, against estimates of $0.64

A non-GAAP operating margin of 28%, up from 23% a year earlier

But it guided fourth-quarter revenue to $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion, growth of 25% to 26%.

Going into the report, analysts expected revenue to keep climbing through 2028:

Datadog (DDOG): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

The 23% growth they expect for 2027 is below even the fourth quarter's guided pace.

Datadog guides low, then beats

Datadog's revenue has risen every quarter for two years:

Datadog (DDOG): total revenues, $ millions, last 8 quarters (to June 30, 2026) (TIKR)

The third quarter added another $76 million. Datadog had guided it just $14 million to $24 million above the second quarter, and beat the top of that range by $52 million. In each of the three quarters before, it had beaten the top of its range by $37 million to $45 million.

My read: the flat fourth-quarter outlook is the same caution.

Dynatrace's revenue grew 17% to $580 million in the quarter ended Sept. 30, and it guided the next quarter higher, to $591 million to $596 million. If spending were slowing across the market, I'd expect that outlook to be flat too.

Cloudflare reports Thursday. It guided third-quarter revenue to $736 million to $737 million, up from $696.1 million in the second quarter. Will its fourth-quarter outlook step up, as Datadog's didn't?

title: What Cloudflare Doubters Overlooked
detail:
What Cloudflare Doubters Overlooked
Bailey Pemberton
Tue, November 3, 2026 at 8:13 AM MST 4 min read
NET
Trade NET on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Cloudflare has given investors plenty to argue about this year, from a sector-wide sell off tied to AI worries to later headlines about AI agents, security certifications, and new business models. Investors who held Cloudflare from the start of the year are up 35.3%, including dividends. If you were deciding on 1 January whether to buy, how much weight would you have put on rich valuation versus the early AI and security story already on the table?

The useful thing about a Narrative is that the reasoning is checkable: the assumptions sit beside the argument, and together they imply an estimated Fair Value you can disagree with.

The move put Cloudflare in the middle of this trade. Scan 53 AI infrastructure stocks for other companies exposed to it.

The Two Cloudflare Stories Investors Had To Weigh

The shares cost US$197 at the start, which meant any decision on Cloudflare hinged on which future investors believed in more.

The bullish narrative put fair value at US$209, 6% above the start price. It was built on an assumption of 26.5% annual revenue growth and profit margins rising to 4.6% within three years.

The bearish case pointed to fair value of US$116, 41% below the start price. It warned that rising cybersecurity regulation and hyperscaler pressure could erode margins even if revenue grew 24.8% a year.

NYSE:NET Trailing 12-Month Earnings & Revenue History as at Nov 2026
What The Cloudflare Evidence Actually Tested

Cloudflare's Q2 2026 update showed revenue at US$696.1 million versus US$512.3 million a year earlier, which backed the growth part of the bullish story. Profit went the other way. The firm reported a larger net loss and net margin moved from -9.8% to -24.4%, so the earlier profitability assumptions stayed unproven. Overall, the evidence cut both ways.

The key lesson is simple. When a bullish case leans on margin improvement, you need to track net margin, not just revenue. For any high-growth stock, compare the original margin pathway with each new earnings report and factor in whether that shift is actually turning up in the numbers.

What Cloudflare's Price Already Assumes Today

Cloudflare now trades at US$265, up strongly from US$197 from the start of the year, so any fresh decision leans heavily on what that quote already implies.

The selected Narrative's Fair Value sits below the current price and leans on Cloudflare as a post-quantum security layer rather than a pure quantum winner. A buyer today is effectively assuming that quantum era trust and security demand will justify this price. How does the Narrative's caution on standalone post-quantum revenue factor into that bet?

Key Takeaways

Cloudflare (NET) stock gained approximately 35% in 2026 through November 2, despite falling 28% from its October high as investors reassessed expensive AI and software stocks.

Datadog (DDOG) has also faced selling pressure, with its November 4 earnings report offering an early indication of enterprise cloud demand before Cloudflare reports on November 5.

Cloudflare's second-quarter revenue increased 36% to $696 million, while management raised its full-year revenue guidance to between $2.864 billion and $2.870 billion.

Cloudflare's expanding AI opportunities support its long-term growth outlook, but declining gross margins and a premium valuation make the stock a hold ahead of earnings.

What Happened?

Cloudflare (NET) stock gained approximately 35% in 2026 through November 2, climbing from $197 at the end of 2025 to $265, according to historical closing prices.

However, shares have fallen approximately 28% from their October 6 intraday high of $370 as investors grew increasingly cautious about richly valued AI infrastructure and software companies.

Datadog (DDOG) experienced similar sector pressure, making its November 4 earnings report an important indicator of enterprise cloud demand before Cloudflare reports on November 5.

Cloudflare's underlying business has continued expanding despite the stock's volatility.

First-quarter revenue increased 34% year over year to $639.8 million, exceeding management's guidance. However, non-GAAP gross margin declined to 72.8% from 74.9% in the previous quarter.

The company also announced plans to reduce its workforce by approximately 1,100 employees as it reorganized around AI and automation.

Shares fell approximately 24% on May 8 as investors weighed strong revenue growth against margin pressure and restructuring concerns.

Second-quarter results demonstrated continued momentum, with revenue increasing 36% to $696.1 million.

Management also raised its full-year revenue guidance to between $2.864 billion and $2.870 billion.

CEO Matthew Prince described the company's expanding opportunity in AI-driven Internet traffic, saying: "we are seeing a fundamental rewrite of the Internet for machine-to-machine traffic."

Cloudflare's developer ecosystem has expanded to more than 10 million developers, compared with 7.4 million at the end of the second quarter.

Its infrastructure for AI agents could create new revenue opportunities as websites begin charging automated systems for accessing content.

Meanwhile, Datadog's second-quarter revenue increased 36% to $1.12 billion, while customers generating more than $100,000 in annual recurring revenue increased 23% to approximately 4,720.

Apple sold off post-earnings despite record service revenue of $31.57 billion, as China revenue misses and rising memory costs squeezed margins.

Bank of America slashed Marvell's target from $400 to $225 after its all-stock Lumentum acquisition triggered downgrades for both companies simultaneously.

Wedbush initiated nuclear energy plays OKLO and X-Energy at Outperform, while Morgan Stanley started autonomous vehicle firm Pony AI at Overweight.

Pre-Market Stock Futures:

Futures are trading mixed early Tuesday, with the Dow Futures down 300 points after yet another tech titan posted outstanding numbers that beat Wall Street estimates, then, like clockwork, sold off in the aftermarket. This time, Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) was the victim; while it was torpedoed after the results were posted, it was still down less than some other mega-cap technology stocks that reported over the last 10 days. iPhone sales were outstanding as demand for the iPhone 18 surged, while service revenue hit an all-time high of $31.57 billion. Reasons for the post-earnings sell-off ranged from the company missing revenue estimates for China to rising costs for memory chips, which are starting to pressure gross margins, which the company lowered for the December quarter. The bottom line is the tech sell-off and investor rotation likely still have a way to go.

After a solid start to the trading week, stocks rolled over after the noon hour, and the same reasons stayed front and center. Massive AI spending and worries about big tech stocks' lack of free cash flow, which in the past had never been an issue, and concerns over the potential for the Democrats to regain the House of Representatives are all contributing to a quiet market sell-off, and with the October jobs report this Friday and the inflation reports next week all still on the burner, those data points will have the ability to move the market.
